where_it_came_from: Two kits belonging to descendants of this line, read at MyHeritage and at 23andMe. The work was done in the Lerena archive, because the tester's father was a Lerena; everything on this page is the half of it that belongs here.
privacy: Both testers are living. Neither is named, and neither is described beyond her position in the descent. The figures kept are the ones that bear on people long dead.

the_two_kits.role: a great-great-granddaughter of the Booyzen line, through her mother
the_two_kits.note: She is roughly half of this family. Her father's side is Argentine and English, which is what makes her useful here: anything Cape in her can only have come through her mother.

the_two_kits.role: her mother's sister - an aunt, on this line and no other
the_two_kits.why_she_matters: She is the instrument. She carries this family's DNA and none of the Argentine or English. Any match shared with her is Cape; any match absent from her list is not. That subtraction has not yet been run, and it is the most valuable unspent thing in this file.

the_cape_signature.reading: Small, and real. West Central African and South Asian together, at trace level, is the ordinary genetic signature of the eighteenth-century Cape - the household slavery the Colony ran on, written into the families that came out of it. In the niece these are halved by her Argentine and English father, so in her mother they are roughly double, and further back they are larger again.
the_cape_signature.care: A trace figure at half a percent is at the edge of what any panel can call, and this archive is not going to convert it into a named ancestor. It is recorded because it is consistent, because it is where this family lived, and because leaving it out would be a choice as much as putting it in.

the_cousinhood_counted.source: 23andMe DNA Relatives, 1,500 closest genetic relatives of the niece.
the_cousinhood_counted.reading: Of the twenty countries named across 1,500 relatives, South Africa is first by a factor of four, and more than half of those name all four grandparents there. This is what a Cape family looks like from the inside.

top_surnames_among_those_relatives.note: The facet shows the top twenty only. It cannot be used to say any surname is ABSENT.

relationship_theories.source: MyHeritage Theory of Family Relativity - a documented path through trees, not a guess from centimorgans.
relationship_theories.reading: Every one of the ten largest theories lands in this family. Booyzen, Barry and Kolbe appear together, which is this archive's own spine arriving unprompted out of somebody else's tree.

the_surname_probe.how_it_was_checked: Two of the six Booyzen hits carry the name only INSIDE their family tree - their own surnames are Bird and Daschner. That is the proof that the search reaches into trees rather than matching the tester's own name, and it is the reason the nulls recorded in the Lerena archive can be trusted.
the_surname_probe.note: These four were run as CONTROLS for a different question, in the Lerena archive. They are recorded here because a control for one question is a finding for another: this family is richly represented in both databases.

what_has_not_been_done: The aunt's own match list has not been harvested. Subtracting it from her niece's is what separates this family's matches from the Argentine and English ones, and it is a day's work, not a discovery.
23andMe's Parental Inheritance, which would split the niece's ancestry by parent and put the Cape trace definitively on this side, is behind a paid tier.

AutoClusters has been generated for the niece but NOT for the aunt. The aunt's chart would be Cape by definition, and any cluster on the niece's chart with no counterpart on the aunt's belongs to her father.

the_autoclusters.what_it_is: MyHeritage AutoClusters, generated 15 September 2026. The tool groups a tester's DNA matches into blocks that all match each other as well as the tester, so each block is in practice the descendants of ONE ancestral couple. It was run on the niece's kit.
the_autoclusters.result: FOURTEEN CLUSTERS, 107 matches, from 50.6 cM upward. Every single one of them is Cape Afrikaner or British Isles. This is the most concrete thing in the whole DNA file for this archive: fourteen ancestral couples, sorted for you, out of a database rather than out of a register.
the_autoclusters.the_one_that_is_this_spine: Cluster 7 is the one to start on - six matches from 56 to 333 cM, the largest match on the whole chart among them, carrying Butler, Daniel and Daschner. Those are the trees in which Booyzen, Booysen and Barry appear together as ancestral surnames.
the_autoclusters.why_it_can_be_trusted: The niece's SON was clustered on the same night as a control. His father is a Defranceski of Istria, and his chart throws up two plainly Croatian clusters - Butorac, Pavelich, Jagustin, Krkljes, Racic, Glas - beside the Cape ones. So the tool demonstrably separates a foreign paternal line from this family's when both are present. The fourteen Cape clusters on his mother's chart are not an artefact of the method.
the_autoclusters.what_to_do_with_it: Each cluster is a couple this archive either already has or does not. Take them one at a time, open the trees, and find where they join the spine. Fourteen leads, each one already proved to be blood.
